Think of waves washing over a rock on the beach. The rock is not completely underwater, but water is constantly flowing over it, covering it, surrounding it. That image — of something being flooded or overwhelmed by something that keeps coming — is the heart of what awash means.

In its most direct, physical sense, awash means covered with water or flooded by it. When something is awash, liquid is washing over its surface so completely that the thing is soaked, submerged, or overflowing.

The ship's deck was awash after the storm.
The low-lying fields were awash after days of heavy rain.
She came in from the rain, her face awash with water.

In these examples, water is not just present — it is covering and overwhelming the surface.
The Figurative Meaning (The More Common Use)

This is where the word truly shines, and where you will encounter it most often. In everyday language, awash is used figuratively to mean flooded with or overwhelmed by a large, excessive amount of something — not necessarily water, but anything at all: emotions, money, people, problems, information, you name it.

The idea is the same as the literal one: just like water that floods and covers everything, whatever thing is being described is present in such large quantities that it seems to be pouring in from everywhere.

The internet is awash with misinformation.
After winning the lottery, he found himself awash in money.
The city was awash with tourists during the festival.
Her eyes were awash with tears.
The tech industry is awash with new AI products.

In each case, the thing is not just present — it is present in overwhelming abundance, to the point where it feels like a flood you cannot escape.

This is an important nuance. Awash does not simply mean "a lot of." It carries a stronger feeling than that — a sense that the quantity is so great it is hard to contain, control, or escape. It suggests being surrounded on all sides, submerged, perhaps even helpless against the sheer volume of something.

This is why it works so well with things like emotions, problems, or chaos:

The grieving family was awash with sympathy from the community.

Here, the sympathy is so abundant that it seems to wash over and surround the family, just like a wave. It feels vivid and powerful — more so than simply saying "received a lot of sympathy."

So when a writer or speaker chooses awash, they are deliberately painting a picture of something that feels flooding and immersive, not just plentiful.

This is something many learners miss, so pay close attention.

Awash is almost always used predicatively. That means it comes after a verb like is, was, were, seems, became — not directly before a noun.

✅ The market was awash with fake goods. (correct)
❌ The awash market. (unnatural — almost never said this way)

The prepositions that follow awash are "with" or "in" — both are correct and widely used:

awash with cash
awash in controversy

Both mean the same thing. You can use either one freely.
How It Differs From Similar Words

You might wonder: how is awash different from words like full, flooded, overflowing, or teeming?

  • Full is neutral — it just means capacity is reached. A glass that is full is not dramatic.
  • Flooded is strong but more about an unwanted event, often with a negative tone.
  • Overflowing suggests spilling past the edges of a container.
  • Teeming suggests a swarm of living things (teeming with ants, teeming with life).
  • Awash is unique because it evokes the image of waves constantly washing over something — a dynamic, ongoing, immersive flood. It works equally well for positive things (awash with praise), negative things (awash with debt), and neutral things (awash with options).

What it meansCovered, flooded, or overwhelmed by a large, excessive amount of something
Literal useCovered with water or liquid
Figurative useHaving an overwhelming abundance of something — emotions, people, things, problems, etc.
Key nuanceNot just "a lot" — suggests a flood-like, immersive, inescapable quantity
Followsa linking verb (is/was/were/became) + with or in

Once you understand the wave image at its core — something washing over and flooding a surface — every use of awash will immediately make sense to you, no matter the context.
